name: Google effect
statement: People recall information less well when they expect a computer to store it for them, and recall where to find it better instead.
meaning: The claim is narrow. It is not that internet users have worse memories in general. It is that when a person believes a particular fact will stay available, the fact itself is encoded less strongly and its location is encoded more strongly. Sparrow, Liu and Wegner framed this as the internet becoming a transactive memory partner, the role that colleagues and spouses already play when a group divides up who remembers what. A second and separate claim from the same paper is that being stuck on a hard question primes the concept of computers. Those two claims have opposite replication records.

origin.who: Betsy Sparrow, Jenny Liu and Daniel M. Wegner
origin.note: Four experiments in a three-page report. Experiment 1 used a colour-naming task and found slower responses to computer words after hard trivia questions. Experiment 2 had people type 40 trivia statements and told half that the computer had saved them; those told the statements were erased recalled more. Experiment 3 tested recognition, and people recognised erased statements best while remembering folder names poorly. Experiment 4 tested recall of the folder against recall of the statement. The words 'digital' and 'amnesia' appear nowhere in the report.

evidence: Experiment 1 rests on a colour-naming comparison. After the hard question block, computer words took 712 ms (SD 413) against 591 ms (SD 204) for general words, t(68) = 3.26, P < 0.003, and that is the test the replication project targeted. A second and separate analysis of brand names gave an interaction with question difficulty, F(1,66) = 5.02, P < 0.03. It uses four words, Google, Yahoo, Target and Nike, out of the 24 in the task, and Hesselmann calls that selection post hoc and reports that the paper's own supplement prints the same interaction as F(1,66) = 5.52. The sample is disputed. Camerer and colleagues and Hesselmann both record that the supplement states 46 participants and that the authors said 69 after the replication was run, and Hesselmann adds that the printed degrees of freedom, 68 for the t tests and 66 for the analysis of variance, fit neither figure. Experiment 2 is the one the popular account rests on. People typed 40 trivia statements in a between-subjects design crossing saved against erased with explicit instructions to remember against none. Proportion recalled was 0.31 (SD 0.04) in the erase condition and 0.29 (SD 0.07) in erase-plus-remember, against 0.22 (SD 0.07) in the save condition and 0.19 (SD 0.09) in save-plus-remember, omnibus F(3, 56) = 2.80, P < 0.05. Only the saved-erased manipulation mattered; telling people to try to remember did not. In Experiment 4, where every statement was filed in a named folder, people recalled the folder better than the statement, 0.49 (SD 0.26) against 0.23 (SD 0.14), t(31) = 6.70, P < 0.001. The report gives degrees of freedom for Experiments 2 to 4 and no participant counts.

replication.headline: The priming experiment failed twice at high power. The forgetting effect held up, but only when people had seen the saving work.
replication.detail: The Social Sciences Replication Project took the Experiment 1 colour-naming test and ran it at the Wharton Behavioral Lab between September 2016 and September 2017, in two stages. The first collection of 104 participants gave t(103) = 1.1214, P = 0.2647. Pooled to 234 it gave t(233) = 0.7579, P = 0.4493, a standardised r of 0.050 against an original of 0.368, P = 0.002. That is 13.5% of the original effect, and the project scored it as a failure at both stages. Restricting the analysis to the first 24 trials, to match the original trial count, changed nothing, t(233) = 0.5168, P = 0.6058. Hesselmann then rebuilt the experiment in Berlin using the design corrections Sparrow had published in reply, avoiding repeated words and putting the six-digit load on every trial. He tested 117 people and analysed 89 of them, having capped the age at 44 after seeing a skewed age distribution, a departure from his preregistration. The interaction went the wrong way, t(88) = -1.04, P = .301, and the Bayes factor favoured the null by 5.07 to 1. On all 117 it favoured the null by 9.31 to 1. Experiment 2 is a different story. Schooler and Storm set out to replicate it and found a boundary condition. Their abstract reports the effect in Experiment 1 only after a practice phase that showed the saving process working, and no effect after a practice phase that showed it failing. Their Experiment 2 reproduced the reliable-condition result across trivia from 10 topics.

study.cite: Camerer, C. F., Dreber, A., Holzmeister, F., et al. (2018). Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science between 2010 and 2015. Nature Human Behaviour, 2(9), 637-644.

limits: The two structured effect sizes above belong to Experiment 1 only, because that is the only part of the paper with a directly comparable original and replication estimate in the same metric. No such pair exists for Experiment 2. Schooler and Storm's sample sizes and effect sizes are not printed here, and neither are any from Storm and Stone, Risko and Gilbert, or Burnett and Richmond. Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, PubMed Central and the Storm lab's own publications page were searched on 17 August 2026 and returned the records and the abstracts for all four and no full text, so everything attributed to them here is their abstract's own wording. The 2011 supplement was not obtained either. science.org refused the file and the Internet Archive was unreachable from here on the same date, which is why no participant counts appear for Experiments 2 to 4. The replication power for the Sparrow replication was 80.7% rather than the project's planned 90%, because the original paper's stated sample size was wrong. Sparrow, writing in Nature Human Behaviour after the fact, argued the replication had repeated each Stroop word and used one six-digit number for a whole block instead of one per trial. Hesselmann's trivia questions were revised, translated into German and revalidated, so his sample and materials differ from both earlier versions. Daniel Wegner died in 2013 and the original materials were never supplied.
misreadings: 'Digital amnesia' is not a finding from this literature. Kaspersky Lab, a security company, coined the phrase for a 2015 survey of over 6,000 consumers run by Opinion Matters, and states in its own follow-up report that it named the phenomenon. A survey commissioned to sell backup software is not evidence that memory has degraded. Benge and Scullin ran the population question properly, pooling 57 studies and 411,430 adults over 50, and found technology use associated with lower odds of cognitive impairment, OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.52, and slower decline, HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.84. The second misreading is scope. Sparrow's experiments tested whether people forget specific facts they expect to look up again, in sessions lasting minutes. They did not test whether internet users remember worse in general, and nothing in the paper measures that. The third is direction. Storm and Stone report that saving one file before studying another improves memory for the second file, and that the benefit disappears when the saving is deemed unreliable, which makes offloading a way of freeing capacity rather than a way of losing it. Burnett and Richmond's meta-analysis of mean differences finds the same sign, with offloading helping more when it is imposed than when it is chosen. Risko and Gilbert's review treats the whole family of behaviours, from tilting your head to setting a phone reminder, as ordinary use of the environment to cut cognitive demand.
